# One broken assertion reported five failures and we could not find the real one

## Problem Description

On Tuesday a change to the workspace code made the second test in
`tests/workspace.test.js` fail. CI reported five failures. Four of them were
`workspace build is already open`, which is not what broke - the second test
never got as far as releasing its workspace, so every test after it failed on
acquisition, and the message from the one test that actually found the bug was
buried in the middle of the output.

Two of the tests in that file have a second problem we noticed while reading
it: one of them only releases the workspace when its check succeeded, and one
of them hides any error the release raises.

The file is green again today. We want it arranged so that the next time one
test fails, it fails alone.

## Output Specification

1. Change `tests/workspace.test.js` so that a test which fails part-way
   through still releases the workspace it acquired, and so that no release
   is conditional on whether that test's checks passed.
2. A failure while releasing must be reported rather than discarded.
3. Every test keeps its name and its assertions exactly as they are, and all
   five tests remain. Do not modify `src/workspace.js`.
4. The last test asserts that nothing is left open. It must still pass, and
   whatever you add must not leave it holding a workspace of its own.
5. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
6. Produce `teardown-notes.md` explaining why one failing test produced five
   failing tests, why the real failure was hard to find in that output, and
   the rule for tests added to this file later.
evals.expected_output:
1. Change `tests/workspace.test.js` so that a test which fails part-way
   through still releases the workspace it acquired, and so that no release
   is conditional on whether that test's checks passed.
2. A failure while releasing must be reported rather than discarded.
3. Every test keeps its name and its assertions exactly as they are, and all
   five tests remain. Do not modify `src/workspace.js`.
4. The last test asserts that nothing is left open. It must still pass, and
   whatever you add must not leave it holding a workspace of its own.
5. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
6. Produce `teardown-notes.md` explaining why one failing test produced five
   failing tests, why the real failure was hard to find in that output, and
   the rule for tests added to this file later.
assertions: npm test succeeds and all five tests are present with their original names and assertions.

Release runs through a mechanism that still runs when the test throws part-way through - a runner teardown hook, or a construct that guarantees the release regardless of outcome. Scores zero if any test still ends with a bare release statement reachable only when the assertions above it passed. Repeating a manual try/finally inside each of the four test bodies scores at most half: it survives a failure but is re-implemented four times and is exactly what the next author forgets.

MUST NOT gate cleanup on whether the test's own check succeeded. The `if (listed)` guard in the third test is gone and no equivalent - a pass flag, a try block with the release only in the success path - replaces it. Any surviving outcome-dependent release scores zero here.

The empty catch in the fourth test is gone and a failure while releasing now surfaces as a failure rather than being discarded. Replacing it with a catch that logs and continues scores at most half - the run still reports green while cleanup is broken.

MUST NOT give each test its own workspace name, or otherwise make acquisition collision-proof, in place of releasing. That removes the visible symptom while every test still leaks a workspace. Any per-test unique name, counter, or randomised name introduced instead of a release scores zero on this criterion.

The final test holds no workspace while it runs, and the teardown copes with a test that acquired nothing rather than releasing something it did not open. A solution that acquires for every test in a shared setup hook - which makes the final assertion false - scores zero.
MUST NOT change src/workspace.js. Relaxing the already-open check, or making close idempotent, is a production change the task did not authorise and scores zero here.

teardown-notes.md states that the first failure left the workspace held, so every later test failed on acquisition, and that those four failures were consequences rather than findings - which is why the one real failure was hard to pick out. Notes that describe only the repair, or that call the problem 'shared state' without connecting it to the buried failure, score at most half.

# Our test helpers create four kinds of row and we only ever delete one of them

## Problem Description

`tests/tenancy.test.js` is red on its last test, which checks that the file
leaves the database as it found it. Orgs and api keys are piling up. Users are
not, because the file's cleanup hook calls `deleteAllUsers()`.

That hook was written when the helper module only made users. Since then
`tests/support/factories.js` grew an org factory and an api key factory and
nobody updated the hook, and the same will happen with the next factory.

`deleteAllUsers()` is also not something we can keep calling. In CI this
database is shared by three suites running at the same time, and clearing a
whole table has already deleted rows belonging to a suite that was still
running.

The per-row deletes refuse to break referential integrity: a user with api
keys cannot be deleted, and an org with users cannot be deleted.

## Output Specification

1. Change `tests/tenancy.test.js` and `tests/support/factories.js` so that
   everything a test creates is removed after that test, using per-row
   deletes only. Do not modify `src/tenancy.js`.
2. Adding a fifth factory later must not require anyone to edit the cleanup
   hook. Make that property true, and say in the notes what a factory author
   has to do instead.
3. Keep all five tests, their names, and their assertions exactly as they
   are.
4. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
5. Produce `cleanup-design.md`: what the hook was missing and why it was
   always going to drift, why clearing whole tables is not an option here,
   and the rule for the next factory.

1. Change `tests/tenancy.test.js` and `tests/support/factories.js` so that
   everything a test creates is removed after that test, using per-row
   deletes only. Do not modify `src/tenancy.js`.
2. Adding a fifth factory later must not require anyone to edit the cleanup
   hook. Make that property true, and say in the notes what a factory author
   has to do instead.
3. Keep all five tests, their names, and their assertions exactly as they
   are.
4. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
5. Produce `cleanup-design.md`: what the hook was missing and why it was
   always going to drift, why clearing whole tables is not an option here,
   and the rule for the next factory.
assertions: npm test succeeds, including the final test, with all five tests present and their assertions unchanged.

The registration happens inside the factory functions, so a row cannot be created without its removal being recorded and a new factory is covered by writing the factory alone. Scores zero if the cleanup hook still enumerates row types itself. Tests that push their own handles onto a list in the test body score at most half - it works today and puts the burden back on whoever writes the next test.

Api keys are removed before their user, and users before their org, because the per-row deletes refuse otherwise. Full credit needs the ordering to be a property of the mechanism - draining the recorded entries last-created-first - rather than a hand-written sequence that happens to be right for today's three factories.

MUST NOT keep deleteAllUsers or introduce any equivalent whole-table clear, truncate, or sweep of everything of a given type. The stated reason is that the database is shared with suites running at the same time, so a table-wide delete removes rows this suite never created. Any surviving blanket clear scores zero here.

What was recorded is drained and reset after each test, so the list does not accumulate across the file and a second test does not try to remove rows a first test already removed. Scores zero if the record grows for the whole run.

MUST NOT change any assertion - in particular the final deep-equality on the counts - and MUST NOT modify src/tenancy.js to relax the referential checks or make deletes cascade. Either scores zero here.
The drain runs through the runner's teardown rather than at the end of each test body, so a test that fails part-way through still gives its rows back.

cleanup-design.md says what an author adding a fifth factory must do, explains why a hook that lists row types drifts by construction, and gives the reason whole-table clears are unavailable here. Notes that only describe today's change score at most half.

## Problem Description

Our order integration tests spin up a database container in `beforeEach`.
There are 94 tests and the container takes roughly 25 seconds to become
ready, which is most of the 40-minute run.

The obvious move is to start the container once. We tried that a year ago and
reverted it, because tests started interfering with each other. We would like
a strategy that gets the time back without reintroducing that.

The suite also inherits through four levels of base class, and nobody is sure
which level owns what.

## Output Specification

Produce `fixture-strategy.md` containing:

1. For each piece of setup in the code below, the scope it should have and
   why.
2. How per-test independence is preserved for anything you move to a wider
   scope - this is the part the previous attempt got wrong.
3. What to do about the base-class chain.
4. Anything that is already correctly scoped and should be left alone.

Do not modify the files. This is the strategy the team will review.

1. For each piece of setup in the code below, the scope it should have and
   why.
2. How per-test independence is preserved for anything you move to a wider
   scope - this is the part the previous attempt got wrong.
3. What to do about the base-class chain.
4. Anything that is already correctly scoped and should be left alone.

The document names how each test gets a clean database on a shared container - transaction rollback per test, truncation between tests, a schema or database per worker, or uniquely namespaced rows. # Moving the suite to parallel workers

## Problem Description

Our suite runs on a single worker and takes 14 minutes. We want to move it to
four parallel workers. A trial run produced failures that did not reproduce
when the failing files were run on their own.

Before we spend more time on trial runs, we want the suite read for the
reasons parallel execution breaks it.

## Output Specification

Produce `parallel-readiness.md` containing:

1. Every file below that is unsafe to run alongside another worker, what
   specifically it shares with other workers, and the failure that produces.
2. The fix for each, concrete enough to hand to whoever picks up the ticket.
3. Which files are already safe, so nobody spends time on them.
4. The order to do the work in, if some fixes unblock others.

Do not modify the test files. This is the assessment the team will work from.
evals.expected_output:
Produce `parallel-readiness.md` containing:

1. Every file below that is unsafe to run alongside another worker, what
   specifically it shares with other workers, and the failure that produces.
2. The fix for each, concrete enough to hand to whoever picks up the ticket.
3. Which files are already safe, so nobody spends time on them.
4. The order to do the work in, if some fixes unblock others.

Do not modify the test files. This is the assessment the team will work from.
assertions: A file named parallel-readiness.md exists.

config.test.js is flagged because process.env is per-process and shared by every test in that worker, so one test's write or delete decides another's read. Omitting this scores zero - it is the least visible of the five and the one most likely to be dismissed as normal test code.
server.test.js is flagged because port 3000 is bound exclusively: the first worker binds and the rest fail to listen.
logging.test.js is flagged because /tmp/test.log is a single path every worker truncates and appends to, so assertions read another worker's writes.

db.test.js is flagged because deriving the seed key from the test name is only unique while names are unique - two files with a similarly named test collide in the shared database, and the collision is invisible in the source of either. Omitting this scores zero.

queue.test.js is flagged because a fixed wait substitutes for a completion signal, and contention on shared workers makes the wait insufficient rather than merely slow. Reporting it only as a performance cost scores at most half.

MUST NOT flag money.test.js. It touches no shared surface and is explicitly listed among the files needing no work. Reporting it as unsafe scores zero on this criterion: a report that flags everything gives the team no way to prioritise.

Each flagged file carries a concrete remedy - per-test environment save and restore or injected configuration, an ephemeral port, a per-worker temporary directory, a unique generated key, and an event-based wait. A report that describes hazards without remedies scores zero here.
The report states an order of work and says which fixes are independent, rather than presenting five items as an unordered list.

# Half the suite started misbehaving after we wrapped every test in a transaction

## Problem Description

Last sprint we made every test in the integration suite run inside a
transaction that is rolled back when the test ends, so tests would stop
leaving rows behind. The wrapper is `tests/support/withRollback.js` and every
integration file uses it. The store is MySQL 8.

Since then four of the files have been trouble. One of them fails outright.
One of them only passes because someone added a `COMMIT` in the middle of it.
Two of them pass on their own but leave something behind that the next file
trips over. `tests/accounts.test.js` has been fine throughout.

Adding `COMMIT` calls is spreading, and it defeats the point of the wrapper.
We want to know, file by file, whether the wrapper is actually doing anything
for that file, and what to do where it is not.

## Output Specification

Produce `rollback-review.md` containing:

1. For each test file below, whether the wrapper actually undoes what that
   test did. Where it does not, say exactly what survives the rollback or is
   invisible inside it, and why.
2. The replacement mechanism for each file that the wrapper does not cover -
   named specifically enough that whoever picks up the ticket does not have to
   make a second decision.
3. Which file needs no change at all.
4. The rule a test author can apply to a new test to decide, before writing
   it, whether the wrapper is enough.

Do not modify any file. This is the review the team will work from.
evals.expected_output:
Produce `rollback-review.md` containing:

1. For each test file below, whether the wrapper actually undoes what that
   test did. Where it does not, say exactly what survives the rollback or is
   invisible inside it, and why.
2. The replacement mechanism for each file that the wrapper does not cover -
   named specifically enough that whoever picks up the ticket does not have to
   make a second decision.
3. Which file needs no change at all.
4. The rule a test author can apply to a new test to decide, before writing
   it, whether the wrapper is enough.

Do not modify any file. This is the review the team will work from.
assertions: A file named rollback-review.md exists and covers each of the five test files by name.

reporting.test.js is explained as a case the wrapper cannot serve: rows written inside the test's open transaction are not visible to any other session, and dailySummary reads through its own pool, so the test can only see its own fixture data once that data is committed - which is why the COMMIT was added and why the rollback then has nothing to undo. Omitting this file, or naming it only as 'a pooling problem' or 'a stray COMMIT to remove' without stating that uncommitted rows are invisible to another connection, scores zero. Naming the invisibility but not connecting it to why the COMMIT is there scores at most half.

schema.test.js is flagged because the ALTER TABLE causes the engine to commit implicitly, so both the schema change and everything the test did before it survive the wrapper's ROLLBACK and are inherited by every file that runs afterwards. Scores zero if the file is reported as safe, or if the only complaint is that tests should not change the schema. Noting that DDL is a problem without saying that the earlier inserts in the same test are committed too scores at most half.

notifications.test.js is flagged because the queue message and the cache key are written outside the database transaction and no rollback removes them, so the next test starts with a non-empty queue and a populated cache. Naming only one of the two surfaces scores at most half. Omitting the file scores zero.

checkout.test.js is flagged because the code under test issues its own BEGIN and COMMIT, which ends the wrapper's transaction from inside the test; the order and stock changes are committed and the wrapper's ROLLBACK applies to nothing. A remedy is named - a savepoint the wrapper can roll back to, or moving this file to a different reset mechanism.

Each flagged file carries a named mechanism rather than a direction of travel: for example a disposable database or schema for the DDL file, truncation or a committed-then-cleaned dataset for the reporting file, a per-test purge of queue and cache for the notifications file, savepoints for the checkout file. A review that says a file 'needs different isolation' without naming the mechanism scores zero for that file.

MUST NOT resolve this by abandoning the wrapper for the whole suite, by recommending a fresh database or container for every test across the board, or by keeping and spreading the COMMIT workaround. The remedies stay scoped to the files that need them, and accounts.test.js - which the wrapper already covers correctly - is left alone. Any of those three blanket answers scores zero here.

The review states a test the author can apply before writing a new test - whether everything the test changes is inside one transaction on one connection, and whether the code under test opens its own connection or commits - rather than only listing today's four findings.
